description: Developing software to monitor astronauts’ health during space missions by tracking physiological indicators, detecting potential abnormalities, and providing data-driven health insights to support timely medical assessments.
summary:
MMG Orbit Crew Buddy is a health monitoring website for astronauts on long missions. Radiation, isolation, altered gravity and a closed environment can cause immune changes, bone loss, heart problems and behavioral health strain, and crews must often spot these changes in themselves.

Each day an astronaut logs vitals such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, mood, stress, exercise, radiation dose and cabin CO2. A health orbit shows five body systems as planets circling a sun, each changing color with its status. Selecting one gives plain language next steps. Indicator cards show value, trend, status and target.

The software flags unusual readings for medical review, including elevated heart rate, low oxygen saturation and sleep below target. It also catches readings far from the astronaut’s own baseline, and flags can be sent to the flight surgeon with a GMT time.

A separate oxygen tank tracker shows remaining supply, time remaining, consumption trends and refill warnings. It stays apart from the medical readings because tank oxygen and blood oxygen are different things.

Entries are saved on the device. The design blends astronomy and health and works on phones, tablets, laptops and large monitors.
details:
MMG Orbit Crew Buddy is a health monitoring website that helps astronauts check on themselves during long missions. Each day the astronaut enters a quick check-in covering heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, mood, stress, exercise, pain, immune symptoms, radiation dose and cabin CO2. The software compares each value with reference ranges and with the astronaut’s own recent readings. It scores five body systems as Steady, Watch or Act now. These are heart and lungs, immune, bones and muscle, mind and sleep, and radiation and cabin air. Each system comes with plain language next steps. Unusual readings, such as elevated heart rate, low oxygen saturation or sleep below the seven hour target, are flagged for medical review and can be sent to the flight surgeon with a GMT time stamp. A separate oxygen tank tracker estimates remaining supply, time remaining, consumption trends and when a refill is needed.

Benefits

Astronauts get one clear place to see how they are doing, how each reading is trending, and what to do about it. Early drift in sleep, heart rate or mood is caught before it becomes a problem. Tank oxygen is kept apart from blood oxygen, so the two are never confused. Flagging for the flight surgeon means the right people see the right readings.

Intended impact

The project aims to make crews more independent when contact with Earth is slow or limited. It helps astronauts notice problems sooner and act with confidence. It also gives medical teams a clearer, time-stamped record of changes. The same approach could later support remote clinics, polar stations and other isolated work.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The site is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG graphics and a canvas starfield. Readings are saved in the browser on the device, and fonts come from Google Fonts. No special hardware is needed, and it runs on phones, tablets, laptops and large monitors. It was built with the help of Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic. The current version uses manually entered readings and demo data rather than live sensors.

What makes it creative

The health orbit turns body systems into planets circling a sun. They move on elliptical orbits, with inner ones moving faster. Planets change color with status, pause when touched, and open guidance when selected. This makes health data feel like looking at the sky instead of reading a spreadsheet. It also suits the mission setting and makes status quick to read at a glance. The design blends astronomy and health throughout, from the starfield to the tank graphic.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety. Readings use simplified reference ranges, and the app says it is not medical advice and points astronauts to the flight surgeon.
  • Clarity. Each indicator shows a label, value, trend, status and target.
  • Separate oxygen measures. Tank oxygen and blood oxygen are tracked in different sections.
  • Reliability. Data is saved on the device so it works without a connection.
  • Time. Every time is shown in GMT.
  • Readability. The text scales across phones, tablets, laptops and large monitors.
  • Motion. Animation respects reduced motion settings.
  • Fatigue. The daily check-in is short because crews are tired and busy.
dataRefs: NASA-STD-3001, Space Flight Human-System Standard, Volume 1: Crew Health
